newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: Woolworths sees 8.5 pct 96/97 sales growth.
newsitem.headline: Woolworths sees 8.5 pct 96/97 sales growth.

text.p: Australia's largest supermarket group Woolworths Ltd said on Monday it was track for sales growth around 8.5 percent in the year to end-June 1997.
"We expect it to be, what we have been experiencing all through out the current year, which is somewhere in the order of eight (percent), 8.5 to nine percent," Clairs told Reuters.
Woolworths earlier reported a 9.27 percent rise in sales to A$11.79 billion for the 40 weeks ended March 30.
Sales in the 1995/96 year totalled A$13.99 billion.
Clairs said said current year sales levels are going to plan. "That's where it will be, maybe a tad better, but it is where I anticipate it," Clairs said.
He said sales from its newly formed wholesaling division will have no impact on 1996/97 sales.
Woolworths' petroleum business was going better than expectations, he said.

"The seven sites that we have, are trading...a little better than our expectations and has encouraged us to fast-track a little bit faster to try and get down as many (sites) as we get permission for as quickly as possible," he said.
Woolworths has enjoyed double-digit sales growth for most of the 1990s, but sales started to slow in 1995/96 as Australia's inflation rate fall and the retail environment became tougher.
The Sydney-based retailer has an agreement with Burmah Oil to sell refined petroleum product from some of its supermarkets.
"Our objective by the year 2000 is to have 200 of them (petrol outlets), but if we can achieve it sooner rather than later, then that is what our intentions are," Clairs said.
He said it was too early to predict what contribution its petroleum business would make to 1996/97 and 1997/98 profits.

Clairs said food sales had remained strong due to the introduction of more fresh food. However, sales from its in-store delicatessens had been affected by recent withdrawals of contaminated food products.

He said Woolworths had no plans to become more involved in Australia's bank payments system following the recommended changes to the banking industry in the government-commissioned Wallis Inquiry into the finance sector.
"It is certainly not on our agenda to be rushing in," Clairs said. The Wallis inquiry report, released last week, urged Australia's payment system be opened up to non-banking groups.

"We will continue to concentrate on the initiatives that we have announced and get those bedded down and in due course, we will examine the outcomes of Wallis and we will see if there are any opportunities," Clairs said in a telephone interview.
At 11.55 a.m. (0155 GMT), Woolworths shares are one cent higher at A$3.63.
